title: PHP2Shell RCE: How to Stop Post-Exploitation | ARIA AZT
summary: Two critical PHP runtime flaws were exploited before disclosure. Learn how AZT stops payloads, shellcode, privilege escalation and C2 after exploitation.
body_markdown:
A stage-by-stage look at how deterministic endpoint and in-memory trust enforcement


stops


post-exploitation after two critical unauthenticated PHP RCE vulnerabilities


are exploited


Currently, there is a barrage of AI attacks appearing daily to attack IT and OT systems without an end in sight. ARIA is the only vendor that has shown that they can stop these attacks and others without having had to have seen them first. ARIA AZT stops these attacks out of the box without need for updates to the AZT solution. ARIA also is the only vendor able to protect legacy out of support PHP systems where patches are no longer available.


PHP2Shell is the name given to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical memory-safety flaws in the PHP runtime that can be reached by an unauthenticated web request before normal application logic runs. Both are rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, and PHP released emergency fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Amazon Threat Intelligence observed an exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026, four days before public disclosure. AZT does not need to wait for repairs to the vulnerable code. Its value begins when successful exploitation tries to launch a denied executable, stage or load untrusted native code, elevate privileges, tamper with AZT, or establish communications that policy does not allow. \[1\]\[2\]\[3\]


**Critical runtime flaws need patching - and post-exploitation needs enforcement.**


**AZT SECURITY ANALYSIS | OCTOBER 2026**


****


# 1. Incident in Brief


On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency security updates for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The flaws affect PHP's request-processing lifecycle itself rather than a particular web application, which means an attacker can reach the vulnerable runtime before authentication or application code has a chance to intervene. PHP states that updating the runtime is the only complete fix. \[1\]\[2\]


The fixed upstream releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Older end-of-life branches remain a special concern and require a supported upgrade or a verified vendor backport. Amazon Threat Intelligence reports that PHP2Shell exploitation attempts were already occurring before disclosure and that exploitation rapidly broadened after patches became public. \[2\]\[3\]


# 2. How the PHP2Shell Attack Progresses


The two CVEs take different routes through PHP's memory lifecycle, but they converge on the same security problem: attacker-controlled request data can corrupt trusted PHP state and redirect legitimate code for an attacker-chosen purpose. The initial takeover can happen without dropping a new executable, modifying PHP's code pages, or injecting shellcode.


## 2.1 An unauthenticated request reaches PHP before the application


The attack begins with a crafted web request sent to an internet-facing PHP service. Public guidance identifies PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed as potentially exposed. Because the vulnerable parsing and request-lifecycle code executes before normal application logic, a login page, CMS permission check, or secure application framework cannot reliably stop the exploit. \[2\]\[4\]


## 2.2 Two memory-corruption paths can produce code execution


CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory corruption flaw. PHP can exhaust its configured memory while request data is only partially initialized; later cleanup then treats invalid state as legitimate. CVE-2026-109619 involves request-owned state that survives after its backing memory has been freed and can be reused by a later request handled by the same worker. Both are runtime memory-lifecycle failures inside trusted PHP. \[2\]\[4\]


## 2.3 Trusted PHP control flow is redirected


This is the key distinction for AZT. The attacker-controlled bytes can remain data in the PHP heap until trusted PHP code interprets them as internal objects, pointers, or call structures. A successful exploit can then redirect execution into code that is already present and trusted - for example, an existing libc function used to launch a command.


## 2.4 The exploit can launch a shell or another child process


A common post-exploitation outcome is command execution through an existing function such as system(), which in turn launches a command interpreter or utility. NO_TRUST evaluates the executable that is actually started. If that shell or utility is denied by effective AZT policy, the process launch is blocked even though the PHP memory exploit itself already succeeded.


If a trusted shell is intentionally allowed, AZT does not infer malicious intent from the command line alone. The next major opportunity comes when the attacker tries to download, write, load, or execute new native code - a common step when turning a one-shot web RCE into persistence, cryptomining, ransomware, credential theft, or a durable remote-access implant.


## 2.5 Follow-on payloads turn an RCE into a server compromise


After gaining command execution, an attacker may stage an ELF binary implant, shared object, downloader, reverse-shell utility, credential tool, or memory-resident payload. They may also attempt to elevate from the web-service account to root, alter local security controls, or establish outbound command-and-control. These later stages create the strongest AZT enforcement points because the attack must introduce or execute code, cross a privilege boundary, or use network paths governed by policy.


# 3. Where AZT Stops PHP2Shell Follow-On Activity


AZT does not need to identify the two PHP CVEs by signature. It enforces deterministic boundaries after exploitation: denied executables do not start, recognized untrusted native payloads cannot be staged or loaded through covered paths, covered privilege escalation is blocked, AZT's own protected resources resist tampering, and prohibited network connections are denied.


## 3.1 Stop 1: NO_TRUST blocks denied shells and untrusted attacker tools


When a successful PHP2Shell exploit attempts to start a new process, AZT performs a trust decision on the executable being launched. An attacker-provided downloader, implant, miner, ransomware binary, credential dumper, or other native tool without an approved TrustID is denied in Enforce/Prevent mode.


- NO_TRUST: blocks execution of untrusted or explicitly blocked executable code at process startup.
- Result: the attacker may corrupt PHP memory, but an untrusted follow-on executable cannot become an active process on the protected server.
- WRITE_BUF: blocks recognized untrusted executable content before a covered write reaches disk.
- READ_BUF: blocks covered reads or loads of untrusted executable content, including the Linux shared-library loading role documented for this control.
- REF_INJ: blocks covered later-stage injected executable images that do not have a valid trust context.
- SHELLCODE: blocks detectable shellcode introduced into memory on supported architectures.


## 3.2 Stop 2: block native payload staging and loading


Attackers commonly convert web-server RCE into a durable compromise by writing or loading native code. AZT provides several enforcement boundaries before that payload can become active.


## 3.3 Stop 3: block privilege escalation and protect AZT enforcement


PHP2Shell initially executes with the privileges of the PHP/web-service worker. If the attacker then attempts a covered Linux privilege transition toward root, PRIV_ESC provides another enforcement point. AZT Self Protect separately denies covered attempts to alter AZT's protected files, resources, configuration, registry-equivalent state, or Trust Store, preserving the controls that stop later stages.


## 3.4 Stop 4: restrict command-and-control and exfiltration


A compromised web server often needs an outbound connection to retrieve tooling, open a reverse shell, establish C2, or exfiltrate data. NPE/BLOCKED_ADDRESS can deny destinations and flows that are prohibited by the deployed network policy. NO_TRUST simultaneously blocks unapproved native networking tools. This is especially valuable after an internet-facing exploit because the attacker cannot assume that successful RCE automatically grants unrestricted outbound reach.


****


# 4. Why PHP2Shell Makes the Case for AZT


## 4.1 A zero-day does not make attacker code trusted


PHP2Shell is a strong example of why vulnerability prevention and executable trust are different layers. A previously unknown flaw can redirect a trusted PHP worker, but that does not grant a TrustID to the attacker's next payload. When the exploit needs a new executable, shared object, injected image, or shellcode-bearing stage, AZT applies the same trust policy whether the original entry point was known yesterday or discovered five minutes ago.


## 4.2 AZT protects the post-exploitation boundary


The first memory-corruption step can occur entirely inside trusted PHP and libc code. AZT's strongest value is therefore not a claim that it repairs PHP's heap. It is that a successful runtime exploit still does not automatically receive permission to execute arbitrary native tools, write and load implants, become root, disable AZT, or connect anywhere it chooses.


## 4.3 Patching and deterministic enforcement work together


PHP explicitly states that there are no complete mitigations for the underlying vulnerabilities: organizations must update PHP and restart the running workers. AZT complements that fix by enforcing the actions an attacker commonly needs after exploitation. Patching closes the vulnerable door; AZT limits what can happen if a new door is discovered later. \[1\]\[2\]


# 6. Conclusion


PHP2Shell shows how dangerous a runtime-level flaw can be: the attacker does not need a vulnerable WordPress plugin, stolen password, or application bug. A crafted request can reach PHP before the application starts and corrupt internal state inside a trusted process. That is why the PHP project describes upgrading as the only complete fix. \[1\]\[2\]


AZT changes the next part of the story. NO_TRUST stops denied shells and untrusted attacker executables. WRITE_BUF and READ_BUF stop covered native payload staging and loading. REF_INJ and SHELLCODE provide additional barriers when the attacker introduces executable code directly into memory. PRIV_ESC blocks covered privilege transitions, AZT Self Protect preserves enforcement, and NPE/BLOCKED_ADDRESS can deny unauthorized follow-on communications. AZT does not replace the PHP patch - it adds deterministic enforcement around the post-exploitation chain so one runtime flaw does not end-up allowing full server control.
